title: Where is it? The ending -da and the missing verb "to have"
goal: Say where things are with the ending *-da*, use *bor* and *yoʻq*, and express ownership as "there is … at me" — because Uzbek has no verb "to have" at all.
bekal: use *bor* / *yoʻq* to say something is there or isn't
say "I have" as *Menda … bor* — literally "at me … there is"

dialogs.title: Dialog — Chorsu bozori qayerda?
dialogs.intro: Budi is lost near Tashkent's old town. He walks up to an older man sitting in front of his shop.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Excuse me, sir. Where's Chorsu Bazaar?

lines.speaker: Aka:
lines.text: Bozor bu yerdan uzoq emas. Metro bekati yonida.
lines.id: The bazaar isn't far from here. It's next to the metro station.
lines.literal: bazaar this place-from far not. metro stop-its side-its-at.

lines.speaker: Aka:
lines.text: Anavi katta masjid oldida. Koʻring, gumbazi koʻk.
lines.id: In front of that big mosque. Look, its dome is blue.
lines.literal: that-over-there big mosque front-its-at. look, dome-its blue.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I see. Is there a bank near here?

lines.speaker: Aka:
lines.text: Ha, bor. Bozorning ichida bank ham bor, dorixona ham.
lines.id: Yes, there is. Inside the bazaar there's a bank, and a pharmacy too.
lines.literal: yes, there-is. bazaar-of inside-its-at bank also there-is, pharmacy also.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thank you! Do you have a phone number?

lines.speaker: Aka:
lines.text: Menda telefon bor, lekin raqamim yodimda yoʻq.
lines.id: I have a phone, but I don't remember my number.
lines.literal: me-at phone there-is, but number-my memory-my-in there-isn't.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Muammo yoʻq. Bu yerda doʻkoningiz bormi?
lines.id: No problem. Is your shop here?
lines.literal: problem there-isn't. this place-at shop-your there-is-?

lines.speaker: Aka:
lines.text: Ha, mana — eshik yonida. Choy bor, marhamat!
lines.id: Yes, there it is — next to the door. There's tea, please come in!
lines.literal: yes, here — door side-its-at. tea there-is, please!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Katta rahmat, aka. Siz juda mehribonsiz.
lines.id: Thank you so much, sir. You're very kind.
lines.literal: big thanks, brother. you very kind-you-are.

notes: **Chorsu bozori, not "bozor Chorsu".** When two nouns are joined — Chorsu Bazaar, metro station, phone number — the **second** one gets the ending *-i*: *bozor**i***, *bekat**i***, *raqam**i***. Like English "Chorsu Bazaar", the name comes first; the extra *-i* is the only new part.

**Place words attach after the thing.** *Yon* (side) → *yonida* (at its side), *old* (front) → *oldida*, *ich* (inside) → *ichida*. These are all nouns with the possessive *-i* and the locative *-da* — not prepositions.

**Anavi = "that one over there".** A pointing word that's farther and more emphatic than *u*. It's often used while pointing with your chin or hand. Its counterpart is *manavi* ("this one right here").
**Yodimda yoʻq = "it's not in my memory".** Uzbek treats memory as a place: *yodimda bor* (I remember), *yodimda yoʻq* (I've forgotten). The same way of thinking comes back in unit 17 for pain.
**Mehribonsiz = "you are kind".** The predicate ending from unit 1 is already at work here. *Mehribon* comes from Persian: *mehr* (love, kindness) + *bon* (keeper) — literally "keeper of kindness".

grammars.title: -da: one ending for "in", "at", and "on"
body: The first of six endings that do the job of English prepositions. Its form **never changes** — whatever the vowels in the word, it's always *-da*.
after: If the noun already has a possessive ending, *-da* comes **last**: *xona-m-da* (in my room), *uy-ingiz-da* (at your house), *qishloq-lar-i-da* (in their villages). The order is fixed: **noun → plural → possessive → place**.
The question word is *qayerda* — literally "what-place-at". One word with *-da* is enough to answer: *Qayerdasiz?* — *Uydaman.* (Where are you? — I'm at home.)

For "on the table" and similar phrases, there are two layers: **[thing]-ning [position]-i-da**. *stolning ustida* (on top of the table), *uyning oldida* (in front of the house), *bozorning ichida* (inside the bazaar). It looks long, but the shape is always the same.

grammars.title: Bor, yoʻq, and owning disguised as "being there"
body: Uzbek has no verb "to have" — not because it's missing something, but because it chose another route. Owning something is expressed as that thing being located somewhere, and that "somewhere" is the owner.

head: Uzbek sentence
Literally
What it means
rows: There's no table in the room.

after: Look at the last two rows: for **things you can carry** you use *[person]-da … bor*, but for **family, body parts, and things that are part of you** you just use the possessive ending: *akam bor*, *vaqtim bor*, *ishim bor*. The line is loose, and Uzbeks themselves use both.
*Bor* and *yoʻq* are adjectives, not verbs — so they can take the unit 1 endings directly: *Men bu yerdaman* (I'm here), *Bormisiz?* (Are you there?), *Yoʻqman* (I'm not here / I'm not available).
⚠️ Don't mix up *yoʻq* and *emas*. *Yoʻq* = there isn't; *emas* = is not. *Kitob yoʻq* (there's no book) is different from *Bu kitob emas* (this isn't a book).

blocks.text: Say each word twice: once bare, once with *-da*. *Bozor — bozorda. Bank — bankda.* Ten seconds per word, and the locative ending stops being theory.

Notice the ending **-xona**: it means "house, place" and comes from Persian (*khāna*). *Choy* + *xona* = tea place. *Kasal* (sick) + *xona* = hospital. *Mehmon* (guest) + *xona* = guest place, hotel. Once you know this, a dozen new words open up on their own: *oshxona* (kitchen, canteen), *kutubxona* (library), *yotoqxona* (dormitory).

⚠️ *Doʻkon* (shop) comes from the Arabic *dukkān* (stall), and the same word turned into *dükkân* in Turkish and *dukan* in Hindi-Urdu. If you've ever haggled in a Middle Eastern market, it may already sound familiar.

sections.title: Showing position: eight words are enough

blocks.text: They all use the same pattern: **[thing]-ning [position]-ida**.
In fast speech, *-ning* is often dropped: *masjid yonida* sounds just as correct as *masjidning yonida*. What you **can't** drop is the *-i-da* ending on the position word.
Two distance words round it off: *yaqin* (near) and *uzoq* (far). *Bu yerdan uzoq emas* = not far from here. *Bozor yaqin* = the bazaar is close.

items: The bank is next to the mosque.
